issues.legal_issue: A caretaker or agent who holds property on behalf of its owner has no independent possessory right to maintain an injunction suit against that owner.
material_facts: The claimant had established title to the property through the pleadings and documents, including records of the proceedings in which the property was acquired.
The opposing occupant did not claim title and failed to prove the alleged family arrangement under which he said he was entitled to occupy the property.
The property had been entrusted to the occupant to look after it while the owner was away, and the occupant was acting as a caretaker.
The occupant sued for an injunction against the title-holder.
issues.conclusion: The caretaker's injunction suit against the true owner was not maintainable, and the caretaker was required to hand over possession on demand.
issues.legal_principle: A caretaker, agent or servant holds property on behalf of the principal and acquires no independent right or interest in it, regardless of the length of the occupation. Such an occupant cannot maintain a suit against the principal on the basis of that possession. The Court relied on Puran Singh v. The State of Punjab (1975) 4 SCC 518 and Mahabir Prasad Jain v. Ganga Singh (1999) 8 SCC 274, and applied the principles in Rame Gowda v. M. Varadappa Naidu (2004) 1 SCC 769 and Southern Roadways Ltd. v. S.M. Krishnan (1989) 4 SCC 603.

predicates.caretaker_or_agent_occupation: The occupant entered or remained in the property as a caretaker or agent holding it on behalf of another person.
predicates.owner_has_established_title: The person seeking possession established title to the property.
predicates.injunction_suit_against_owner: The occupant brought an injunction suit against the person who established title.

issues.definition: When an occupant holds property as a caretaker or agent for a person whose title is established, an injunction suit by the occupant against that person is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: An occupant who seeks to remain in property after another person establishes title must plead and document a sufficiently particularized basis for the claimed right to continue in possession.
material_facts: The title-holder's pleadings and documents established title to the property.
The occupant claimed a right to remain in possession but did not establish title or prove the alleged family arrangement.
The occupant's asserted basis for continuing in possession was not supported by sufficiently particularized pleadings and documents.
issues.conclusion: The occupant had not established a basis to continue in possession; the courts must require sufficient particulars and supporting documents before framing an issue for trial on such a claim.
issues.legal_principle: Where pleadings and documents establish title and continued possession is disputed, the person resisting recovery or claiming a right to remain must provide detailed pleadings, particulars and supporting documents. The Court must examine pleadings and documents before framing issues; vague pleadings do not raise an issue and may justify rejection of the claim or a decree on admission. The Court also emphasized discovery and production powers under Section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: civil_possession_dispute and claimant_established_title and occupant_claims_right_to_remain and occupant_lacks_specific_pleadings_or_supporting_documents

predicates.civil_possession_dispute: A civil proceeding concerns recovery of property or a claimed right to remain in possession.
predicates.claimant_established_title: The person seeking recovery established title to the property through pleadings and documents.
predicates.occupant_claims_right_to_remain: The person in occupation asserts a right to continue in possession.
predicates.occupant_lacks_specific_pleadings_or_sup: The occupant does not provide sufficiently detailed particulars and documents supporting the asserted right to remain.

issues.definition: If title is established in a civil possession dispute and the occupant's asserted right to remain lacks specific pleadings or supporting documents, the unsupported claim may be rejected without framing an issue.

issues.legal_issue: A judicial determination of the parties' rights in a competent court satisfies the requirement of due process, even when the proceeding is brought by the person seeking protection from dispossession.
material_facts: The occupant brought a suit seeking an injunction against dispossession.
A competent court adjudicated the parties' rights in that proceeding.
The occupant failed to establish a basis for the protective injunction.
issues.conclusion: Due process was satisfied by the adjudication of the parties' rights in the injunction proceeding; a separate action by the owner to recover possession was not required merely because the occupant's injunction claim failed.
issues.legal_principle: Due process means that a person in settled possession is not forcibly dispossessed without recourse to a court and an adjudication of the parties' rights; it does not require completion of an entire trial in every instance. The Court approved the Delhi High Court's reasoning in Thomas Cook (India) Limited v. Hotel Imperial, 2006 (88) DRJ 545.

predicates.protective_injunction_proceeding: A person in occupation brought a proceeding seeking protection against dispossession.
predicates.competent_court_adjudicated_parties_righ: A court with jurisdiction determined the parties' rights in that proceeding.

issues.definition: When a competent court determines the parties' rights in a proceeding seeking protection against dispossession, that adjudication satisfies due process.

issues.legal_issue: Courts in civil proceedings must actively pursue the truth and use available procedural powers to obtain relevant evidence needed for a just decision.
material_facts: The dispute concerned competing accounts of ownership, possession and the basis on which the occupant entered and remained in the property.
The Court found that the lower courts had failed to properly assess the pleadings and documents relevant to those matters.
The Code of Civil Procedure provides courts with powers concerning discovery, interrogatories, production of documents, summonses and proof by affidavit.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that truth must guide judicial proceedings and that judges must take an active role, within procedural law, in ascertaining relevant facts rather than remaining passive.
issues.legal_principle: Truth is the foundation of justice, and courts have a duty to seek it through an active but legally bounded role in proceedings. Section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides powers for discovery and production of evidence. The Court relied on Mohanlal Shamji Soni v. Union of India, 1991 Supp (1) SCC 271, Ritesh Tewari v. State of U.P. (2010) 10 SCC 677, and Chandra Shashi v. Anil Kumar Verma (1995) 1 SCC 421.

predicates.civil_proceeding: The matter before the court is a civil proceeding.
predicates.material_factual_dispute: The parties' accounts differ on facts that affect the decision.

issues.definition: In a civil proceeding involving a material factual dispute, the court must actively seek the truth within the limits of procedural law.

issues.legal_issue: Courts deciding applications for injunction must carefully assess the pleadings and documents and address the equitable consequences of allowing a party to remain in possession.
material_facts: The occupant obtained and retained the benefit of a court order in a dispute over possession of valuable property.
The lower courts did not adequately assess the pleadings and documents or address the consequences of continued occupation.
The dispute continued for a prolonged period while the title-holder remained out of possession.
issues.conclusion: Courts must scrutinize the record with care when granting or refusing an injunction and should consider pragmatic conditions, including appropriate mesne profits, to balance the parties' interests.
issues.legal_principle: The ordinary principles governing injunctions are a prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury. Courts must carefully examine pleadings and documents, give due consideration to the circumstances of occupation, and may set appropriate mesne profits by reference to prevailing market rentals. The Court also relied on the approach to discouraging frivolous litigation in Ramrameshwari Devi v. Nirmala Devi (2011) 8 SCC 249.

predicates.injunction_application_in_property_posse: An application for injunction concerns possession of property.
predicates.continued_occupation_may_affect_equities: The requested injunction would permit a party to remain in occupation while the dispute is pending.

issues.definition: When an injunction application concerns property possession and continued occupation may affect the parties' equities, the court must scrutinize the record and consider appropriate conditions for occupation.
